Assistant: Congratulations on your pregnancy! That's amazing news! Childbirth can be a bit overwhelming, but with the right knowledge and preparation, you'll be just fine. Let's start with the basics: have you thought about your birth plan?
User: A birth plan? I'm not even sure what that is. Is it like a checklist or something?
Assistant: Ha ha, kind of! A birth plan is a document that outlines your preferences for labor, delivery, and postpartum care. It's a great way to communicate with your healthcare provider about what you want and don't want during the process. We can go over some of the things you might want to consider, like pain management options.
User: Oh, that sounds like a great idea. I've heard horror stories about how painful childbirth can be. What are some of the pain management options available?
Assistant: Well, there are a few different options. Some women prefer to go the natural route, using techniques like deep breathing and massage to manage pain. Others might choose to use medication, like epidurals or narcotics. And then there are some alternative options, like acupuncture and hydrotherapy.
User: Hydrotherapy? That sounds interesting. What's that all about?
Assistant: Hydrotherapy involves using water to help manage pain and discomfort during labor. Some hospitals and birthing centers even offer birthing pools or tubs that you can soak in during labor.
User: Ah, I think I've heard of that! I've heard that water births can be a great option for pain management, but I'm not sure if it's right for me. What are the benefits and drawbacks?
Assistant: Water births can be a fantastic option for some women. The benefits include reduced pain, a more relaxed atmosphere, and even a shorter labor. However, it's not suitable for everyone, especially if you have certain medical conditions or complications during pregnancy. We should discuss your individual situation and see if it's a viable option for you.
User: That sounds great. What kind of medical conditions would rule out a water birth?
Assistant: Women with conditions like preeclampsia, placenta previa, or multiple gestations might not be good candidates for a water birth. Additionally, if you have any infections or other complications during labor, your healthcare provider might recommend a different delivery method.
User: Okay, I think I understand. What about the logistics of a water birth? How does it all work?
Assistant: Well, if you decide to have a water birth, you'll typically get into the birthing pool or tub when your labor is progressing. The warm water can help relax your muscles and reduce pain. You can even bring a support person or two into the pool with you for added comfort. Once the baby is born, the healthcare provider will carefully lift them out of the water and hand them to you for immediate skin-to-skin contact.
User: That sounds like an amazing experience! I'm definitely considering it now. What's the next step?
Assistant: I'm glad you're considering it! Next, we should discuss this option with your healthcare provider to see if it's a good fit for you and your baby. They can assess your individual situation and help you make an informed decision. In the meantime, I can provide you with some resources and information to help you prepare for a water birth, just in case. How does that sound?
User: Hey, I've been hearing a lot about home births lately. What's your take on them?
Assistant: Home births are definitely a growing trend, and for good reason. Many women are looking for a more personalized and intimate experience when it comes to giving birth. But, of course, it's not for everyone. What sparked your interest in home births?
User: I have a friend who recently had a home birth, and she said it was an incredible experience. But I have to admit, I'm a bit skeptical. Is it safe?
Assistant: That's a valid concern. Home births can be safe, but it's essential to have the right support and precautions in place. Typically, women who opt for home births have low-risk pregnancies and work with a trained midwife or healthcare provider who can monitor their progress and intervene if needed.
User: That makes sense. So, what are the benefits of having a home birth?
Assistant: Well, for one, it can be a much more relaxed and peaceful experience. Women can move around freely, eat and drink what they want, and have their loved ones nearby for support. Plus, it can be a more cost-effective option compared to hospital births. But, again, it's crucial to have the right support and medical backup in case of any complications.
User: I see. And what about the different types of home births? I've heard of unassisted and assisted births, but I'm not entirely sure what those terms mean.
Assistant: Ah, great question! Unassisted births, also known as free births or DIY births, are when a woman gives birth at home without any medical assistance. This can be a bit riskier, as there's no trained professional present to handle any potential complications. On the other hand, assisted births involve a trained midwife or healthcare provider who provides support and guidance throughout the birth process.
User: That's really interesting. I'm interested in learning more about the different types of home birth, including unassisted and assisted births. Can you tell me more about what to expect from each?
Assistant: Absolutely. With an unassisted birth, the woman is entirely responsible for her own care and the birth process. This can be a very empowering experience, but it requires a lot of preparation and education. Women who choose unassisted births often do a lot of research and planning to ensure they're prepared for any scenario. On the other hand, assisted births can offer a bit more peace of mind, as there's a trained professional present to handle any complications that may arise.
User: I can see the appeal of both options. But what about the logistics? How do women prepare for a home birth, and what kind of equipment or supplies do they need?
Assistant: Preparing for a home birth involves a lot of planning and preparation. Women typically work with their healthcare provider to create a birth plan, which outlines their preferences for the birth. They'll also need to gather supplies, such as a birthing pool, towels, and comfortable clothing. In terms of equipment, some women may choose to rent a birthing pool or purchase a birth stool. The healthcare provider will also bring their own equipment, such as oxygen and a Doppler for monitoring the baby's heart rate.
User: That sounds like a lot to consider. What about the emotional aspect of a home birth? How do women prepare themselves mentally and emotionally for the experience?
Assistant: Ah, that's a great question. Preparing for a home birth can be an emotional and mental journey, just as much as it is a physical one. Women often do a lot of self-reflection and preparation to get themselves mentally and emotionally ready for the experience. This can involve things like meditation, visualization, and connecting with other women who have had home births. Having a strong support system in place can also make a big difference.
User: I can imagine. And what about the partner's role in a home birth? How can they be involved and supportive?
Assistant: Partners can play a huge role in a home birth, providing emotional support, helping with logistics, and even assisting with the birth itself. Some partners may choose to be more hands-on, while others may prefer to take a more backseat role. It's essential for the partner to be supportive and understanding of the woman's needs and preferences, and to be prepared to advocate for her if needed.

c79-m1.summary: The decision to perform a hysterectomy during the delivery of a baby with placenta accreta or placenta increta depends on several factors, including the severity of the condition, the patient's health, and the desire for future pregnancies.
c79-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Detail the differences between a placenta accreta and a placenta increta.
Assistant: Placenta accreta and placenta increta are both conditions that occur during pregnancy when the placenta grows too deeply into the uterine wall.

Placenta accreta: 

- Occurs when the placenta grows too deeply into the uterine wall but does not penetrate the muscle layer
- Can cause severe bleeding during delivery
- Typically happens in women who have had a previous C-section, as scar tissue from the previous surgery can make the placenta more likely to attach to the uterine wall
- Can be diagnosed before delivery through ultrasound or MRI imaging
- Treatment may involve a hysterectomy (removal of the uterus) after delivery to control bleeding and prevent complications

Placenta increta:

- Occurs when the placenta grows even more deeply into the uterine wall and penetrates the muscle layer
- Can cause severe bleeding and difficulty delivering the placenta
- Is less common than placenta accreta 
- May not be diagnosed until delivery or after delivery through examination of the placenta 
- Treatment may involve a hysterectomy or removal of the affected portion of the uterus, as well as blood transfusions and other supportive measures to manage bleeding and complications. 

Overall, placenta increta is a more severe form of placenta accreta and requires more extensive treatment and monitoring.
User: Is there anything I can do to prevent these conditions?
Assistant: The risk factors for placenta accreta and placenta increta are primarily related to prior uterine surgeries, such as a C-section, or placenta previa, a condition where the placenta implants near the cervix. These conditions increase the likelihood of abnormal placental attachment. However, there are some preventative measures that some doctors recommend, including:

1. Vaginal birth after a prior C-section, if possible, as repeated C-sections raise the risk of these conditions. 2. Avoiding unnecessary uterine surgeries, if possible. 3. If you have placenta previa, you may be advised to avoid activities that increase the risk of bleeding, such as sex or exercise. 4. Finally, receiving early and regular prenatal care can help ensure that any potential issues, such as abnormal placental attachment, are diagnosed and managed as early as possible. Ultimately, whether or not you can take steps to prevent placenta accreta or placenta increta may depend on your individual risk factors and medical history, so be sure to discuss any concerns with your doctor.
User: Thanks for sharing those tips, I'll definitely keep them in mind for my next pregnancy. Do most women with placenta accreta or increta require a hysterectomy?
Assistant: The decision to perform a hysterectomy during the delivery of a baby with placenta accreta or placenta increta depends on several factors, including the severity of the condition, the patient's health, and the desire for future pregnancies. In some cases, it may be possible to remove the placenta and preserve the uterus. However, in more severe cases, a hysterectomy may be necessary.

Studies have shown that the rate of hysterectomy for placenta accreta or increta is high, ranging from around 40-60%. This is because of the high risk of hemorrhage during the delivery, and a hysterectomy may be the only way to control bleeding and prevent serious complications.

However, some women may opt for fertility-sparing surgical techniques, such as uterine artery embolization, to preserve their fertility. These options should be discussed with a healthcare provider, who can help weigh the risks and benefits of each approach.

User: Detail the differences between a placenta accreta and a placenta increta.
Assistant: Placenta accreta and placenta increta are both conditions that occur during pregnancy when the placenta grows too deeply into the uterine wall.

Placenta accreta: 

- Occurs when the placenta grows too deeply into the uterine wall but does not penetrate the muscle layer
- Can cause severe bleeding during delivery
- Typically happens in women who have had a previous C-section, as scar tissue from the previous surgery can make the placenta more likely to attach to the uterine wall
- Can be diagnosed before delivery through ultrasound or MRI imaging
- Treatment may involve a hysterectomy (removal of the uterus) after delivery to control bleeding and prevent complications

Placenta increta:

- Occurs when the placenta grows even more deeply into the uterine wall and penetrates the muscle layer
- Can cause severe bleeding and difficulty delivering the placenta
- Is less common than placenta accreta 
- May not be diagnosed until delivery or after delivery through examination of the placenta 
- Treatment may involve a hysterectomy or removal of the affected portion of the uterus, as well as blood transfusions and other supportive measures to manage bleeding and complications. 

Overall, placenta increta is a more severe form of placenta accreta and requires more extensive treatment and monitoring.

User: How does the neonatal intensive care team at [name of hospital] provide specialized care for premature infants?
Assistant: I do not have access to specific information about hospitals. However, in general, neonatal intensive care teams provide specialized care for premature infants in several ways:

1. Monitoring vital signs: the team closely monitors the infant's heart rate, breathing, and blood oxygen levels using advanced monitoring equipment.

2. Providing breathing support: premature infants often have underdeveloped lungs and require breathing support. The team may provide oxygen therapy or use a mechanical ventilator to help the infant breathe.

3. Nutritional support: premature infants may have difficulty feeding due to underdeveloped digestive systems. The team may administer nutrients through an iv or feeding tube.

4. Preventing infection: premature infants have immature immune systems and are at a higher risk of developing infections. The team takes special precautions to prevent infection, such as limiting visitors and practicing strict hand hygiene.

5. Kangaroo care: skin-to-skin contact with the mother or father known as kangaroo care helps regulate the infant's body temperature, heart rate, and breathing, promoting bonding and healing.

overall, the neonatal intensive care team provides round-the-clock care, including specialized medical equipment and a range of interventions to support the health and development of premature infants.

Birth weight: Low birth weight infants require specialized care as they may have difficulty regulating their body temperature and may require more frequent feedings. 3. User: How does the neonatal intensive care team at [name of hospital] provide specialized care for premature infants?
Assistant: I do not have access to specific information about hospitals. However, in general, neonatal intensive care teams provide specialized care for premature infants in several ways:

1. Monitoring vital signs: the team closely monitors the infant's heart rate, breathing, and blood oxygen levels using advanced monitoring equipment.

2. Providing breathing support: premature infants often have underdeveloped lungs and require breathing support. The team may provide oxygen therapy or use a mechanical ventilator to help the infant breathe.

3. Nutritional support: premature infants may have difficulty feeding due to underdeveloped digestive systems. The team may administer nutrients through an iv or feeding tube.

4. Preventing infection: premature infants have immature immune systems and are at a higher risk of developing infections. The team takes special precautions to prevent infection, such as limiting visitors and practicing strict hand hygiene.

5. Kangaroo care: skin-to-skin contact with the mother or father known as kangaroo care helps regulate the infant's body temperature, heart rate, and breathing, promoting bonding and healing.

overall, the neonatal intensive care team provides round-the-clock care, including specialized medical equipment and a range of interventions to support the health and development of premature infants.
User: Do you know if there are any other factors that can affect the care provided to premature infants?
Assistant: Yes, there are several other factors that can affect the care provided to premature infants. Some of these factors include:

1. Gestational age: The care provided to premature infants may depend on their gestational age at birth. Infants born extremely premature may require more advanced medical interventions, such as surfactant therapy to help with breathing, and specialized nutrition to support their growth and development. 2. Birth weight: Low birth weight infants require specialized care as they may have difficulty regulating their body temperature and may require more frequent feedings. 3. Medical conditions: Premature infants may also have medical conditions such as respiratory distress syndrome, sepsis, and jaundice, which require specialized care and treatment. 4. Parental involvement: The involvement of parents or caregivers in the care of premature infants can have a significant impact on their development and recovery, and neonatal intensive care teams actively encourage and support parents to participate in the care of their baby. 5. Social or environmental factors: Social or environmental factors can also affect the care provided to premature infants. For example, infants born to mothers who have used drugs or alcohol during pregnancy may require specialized care to manage withdrawal symptoms. Similarly, infants born into low-income families may face more challenges in accessing specialized care and support.

1. Skin-to-skin contact: As I mentioned earlier, skin-to-skin contact, also known as kangaroo care, can be beneficial for both the baby and the parents. Parents can hold their infant against their bare chest, which can help regulate the baby's body temperature and breathing and promote bonding.

2. Feeding: Parents can participate in feeding their infant by providing breast milk if possible or helping with bottle feedings for those who are formula-fed.

3. Diaper changes: Parents can change the infant's diaper, which provides a chance for gentle touch, bonding, and getting to know their baby's normal behavior.

4. Bathing: Parents can learn how to bathe their infant with a nurse's supervision and guidance in the NICU.

5. Talking, singing, and reading to the infant: Parents can talk, sing, read stories or provide gentle touch to comfort their baby and promote bonding.

6. Being present: Parents can be present during medical procedures or rounds and can ask questions and express concerns about their baby's care.

The NICU team will also provide education and support to parents on how to participate in their infant's care and prepare them for their baby's transition home.

2. Provide comforting sounds: Premature infants can be soothed by the sound of their parent's voice, music, or white noise. Parents can sing to their infant, read a book, or talk to them to provide comfort.

3. Promote physical touch: Gentle touch is crucial for a baby's development. Parents can provide a gentle touch by holding their infant's hand, massaging their back, or stroking their cheek.

4. Support their baby's feeding: Breast milk is the best nutrition for a premature infant. Parents can work with the NICU team to establish and maintain breastfeeding, provide expressed milk, or offer formula as recommended.

User: Given the text: A Texas judge has ordered that a brain-dead pregnant woman be removed from life support after her husband filed suit against a Fort Worth hospital for "cruel and obscene mutilation" of a dead body.
In a case that has captured national headlines and become a battleground for both sides of the abortion debate, state District Judge R.H. Wallace ordered John Peter Smith Hospital to remove the woman's body from a ventilator by 5 p.m. Monday.
Marlise Munoz, 33, was 14 weeks pregnant when her husband, Erick Munoz, found her unconscious on the floor of their kitchen on Nov. 26, possibly due to a blood clot in one of her lungs.
Although doctors at the county-owned hospital later told the husband that his wife was brain dead and would never recover, the hospital chose to keep her body on life support against the family's wishes, citing a Texas law that prohibits hospitals from suspending "life-sustaining treatment" on patients who are pregnant.
On Friday, lawyers for the husband argued in court that hospital officials had misread the law and said it did not apply to a corpse. They also told the judge that the now 22-week-old fetus was "distinctly abnormal."
[Updated Jan 24, 5:04 p.m. PST: Following the judge's decision, the hospital released a statement saying the JPS Health Network "appreciates the potential impact of the consequences of the order" and would consult with the Tarrant County district's attorney's office, which represents the hospital."
In an affidavit filed in court Thursday, the husband said it was clear to him that his wife was no longer alive.
"When I bend down to kiss her forehead, her usual scent is gone, replaced instead with what I can only describes as the smell of death," Munoz wrote in court papers.
Before Friday's hearing, demonstrators outside the hospital either demanded that the woman's body remain on life support so that the fetus could be kept alive or that the hospital "let Marlise rest in peace."
Just prior to Friday's court hearing, lawyers representing the husband released a statement to the media insisting the 22-week-old fetus was "distinctly abnormal."
"Even at this early stage, the lower extremities are deformed to the extent that the gender cannot be determined," lawyers Heather King and Jessica Hall Janicek wrote.
"The fetus suffers from hydrocephalus [water on the brain]. It also appears that there are further abnormalities, including a possible heart problem, that cannot be specifically determined due to the immobile nature of Mrs. Munoz's deceased body," the lawyers wrote.
"Quite sadly, this information is not surprising due to the fact that the fetus, after being deprived of oxygen for an indeterminate length of time, is gestating within a dead and deteriorating body, as a horrified family looks on in absolute anguish, distress and sadness," the lawyers wrote.
Hospital officials had remained close-lipped about the matter, saying the issue was best decided by a court.
Hospital spokeswoman J.R. Labbe told reporters initially that the hospital was following the law and standing by its decision.
The state law at issue, Texas Health and Safety Code 166.049, states that "a person may not withdraw or withhold life-sustaining treatment under this subchapter from a pregnant patient."
Numerous legal and health experts, however, said that if in fact Marlise Munoz was determined to be brain dead, the law would not apply.
The term "brain death" refers to the irreversible cessation of all functions of the entire brain, including the brain stem, which controls autonomic functions such as breathing and heart rate.
By comparision, patients in a coma or vegetative state have full or partial autonomic brain function and may recover, although the chance of that decreases the longer the condition persists, according to physicians.
Erick Munoz has inisted in court documents that the hospital's conduct has been outrageous.
"One of the most painful parts of watching my wife's deceased body lie trapped in a hospital bed each day is the soulless look in her eyes," he wrote in the court affidavit. "Her eyes, once full of the 'glimmer of life,' are empty and dead. My wife is nothing more than an empty shell. She died in November 2013, and what sits in front of me is a deterioriating body."
RELATED: Q&A: Can brain death be reversed?
Cases of pregnant women who are kept on life support after being declared brain-dead are rare. Researchers from Heidelberg University in Germany searched the medical literature for examples and found only 19 cases from 1982 to 2010.
Twelve of those fetuses were deliverd by caesarean section and survived for some period of time after birth. One of the babies, born prematurely after just 25 weeks of gestation, died of an infection at the age of 30 days. Six of the others were developing normally at the time the case reports were written.
The authors said that because the data were incomplete, there was no way to determine the liklihood that a fetus would survive after its mother suffered brain death.

User: Hey, I've been trying to get into wine lately. Do you know anything about it?
Assistant: Ah, wine! There's so much to explore. What sparked your interest? Are you looking for some recommendations or just wanting to learn more about the basics?
User: Yeah, I guess I just want to learn more about it. I've tried a few different types, but I don't really know what I'm doing. I've heard people talk about tannins and acidity, but it's all a bit lost on me.
Assistant: Don't worry, it's not as complicated as it sounds! Tannins and acidity are just two of the many factors that contribute to a wine's flavor profile. Tannins give wine its dry, puckering sensation, while acidity makes it feel refreshing and crisp. Think of it like a seesaw – a good wine usually finds a balance between the two.
User: That makes sense, I think. So, how do people usually go about learning more about wine? Are there any good resources out there?
Assistant: Absolutely! There are tons of wine books, blogs, and YouTube channels out there. Some people even take wine courses or join wine clubs to learn more. But honestly, one of the best ways to learn is by talking to other wine enthusiasts. You can pick up so much just by hearing about their experiences and recommendations.
User: That's a great idea. I've actually stumbled upon a few online forums where people discuss their favorite wines. I've been thinking about joining in, but I'm not sure if I'd fit in.
Assistant: Ah, online forums can be a fantastic way to connect with like-minded people! What's holding you back from joining in? Is it fear of not knowing enough, or something else?
User: Yeah, I guess it's just that I don't want to sound stupid in front of people who know way more than me. But at the same time, I really want to learn from them!
Assistant: Trust me, most people in online forums are there to share their passion and help others, not to judge. And who knows, you might even discover some new favorite wines or learn something that blows your mind!
User: Alright, you've convinced me! I think I'll take the plunge and start participating in one of the forums I've been lurking on. Actually, there's one in particular that I've been following – it's a community forum for a wine vlog I really enjoy.
Assistant: Ah, nice! Wine vlogs can be so much fun to follow, and having a community aspect to it must make it even more engaging. What do you like most about this particular vlog, and what kind of discussions have you seen on the forum so far?
User: Well, the vlog is really well-produced, and the host has a great sense of humor. As for the forum, I've seen people discussing everything from their favorite wine and food pairings to tips on how to spot a good deal on wine. It's really inspiring to see how passionate everyone is about wine!
Assistant: That sounds like a fantastic community to be a part of! I'm sure you'll fit right in. Do you think you'll start by asking questions, sharing your own experiences, or just seeing where the conversations take you?
User: Hmm, I think I'll start by responding to some of the existing threads and see how it goes from there. Wish me luck!
Assistant: You don't need luck! Just be yourself, be respectful, and have fun. And don't hesitate to reach out if you need any more advice or just want to share your progress. Happy wine exploring!
User: Hey, have you ever tried a Pinot Noir from Oregon? I had one last night that was incredible.
Assistant: Honestly, I'm not much of a wine person. I can't really tell the difference between types and brands.
User: That's okay, it's definitely not for everyone. But if you ever want to try something new, I'd love to recommend a few to you.
Assistant: Maybe I'll take you up on that. So have you ever been on a wine tasting tour?
User: Yes! I actually went to Napa Valley last year with some friends. It was amazing.
Assistant: That sounds fun. I've always wanted to go to a vineyard and see how they make wine.
User: It's definitely worth checking out. You learn a lot about the whole process and get to taste some amazing wines.
Assistant: You know, I've been thinking about trying some more expensive wines lately. Do you have any favorites that you would recommend?
User: Oh, there are so many! It really depends on what kind of wine you like. But one of my favorites is a Cabernet Sauvignon from a winery in California. It's a bit pricier, but totally worth it.
Assistant: I'll have to keep that in mind. Maybe I'll surprise my fiancee with a nice bottle for our anniversary this year.
User: That's a great idea! I'm sure she'll love it. Let me know if you need any help picking one out.

User: I went to a wine tasting last night and it was amazing! I learned so much about different types of wines and how to pair them with food.
Assistant: That's interesting. I've never been to a wine tasting before.
User: You should definitely go to one! It's a great way to learn about different wines and meet new people who share the same interest.
Assistant: I might consider it. So, how did you become interested in wine?

Assistant: That's cool. I remember you talking about your business trip a while ago. It's great that it opened up new interests for you.
User: Yes, it really did. And it's nice to have a hobby that I enjoy and can also share with others. Plus, it's always fun to try new wines and see how they pair with different foods.
Assistant: I can see that. It's like exploring a whole new world of flavors.

Assistant: That sounds like a fun hobby. What got you interested in wine in the first place?

User: Develop a dialogue between two experienced wine makers exploring different approaches to wine production, including methods of grape selection, storage, fermentation, ageing, and bottling. Use descriptive and technical language to convey the intricacies and nuances of the winemaking process, while also providing context on the historical and cultural significance of winemaking. Additionally, touch upon the importance of experimentation and innovation in wine production, as well as the key factors that can impact the final flavour profile of the finished product such as climate, soil, and fermentation vessels. Aim to create a nuanced and engaging discussion that highlights the art and science of winemaking.
Assistant: Winemaker 1: Hey there, it’s great to be able to talk wine with a fellow winemaker. So, let's get right into it. How do you choose the grapes for your wines?

c105-m1.summary: Layne Montgomery plans to build a new winery on a 17-acre site.
c105-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: For the past eight years, the compelling quality of m2 Wines has been all the impetus Lodi wine lovers have needed to beat a path to winemaker/proprietor Layne Montgomery’s unadorned warehouse/winery, on the far eastern side of town along Turner Rd.
Nonetheless, Montgomery thinks it’s high time that he makes a move into a “real winery.” Thus, Montgomery and his original group of partners and investors have announced plans to break ground – as early as this December, if weather and permitting goes well – for a new m2 estate on a triangular 17 acre site south of Peltier Rd., just west of Hwy. 99 along the railroad tracks.
This might be music to the ears of wine lovers who are in it mostly for the wine, not the scene, and who may be tiring of the “ghetto-chic” setting of the current m2 home. Montgomery also admits that, for the new place, he will be applying for the maximum number of special event permits as well, in order to participate in the usual calendar of Lodi wine country events.
Our last visit with Mr. Montgomery (this past October 22) was also a good time to catch up on the latest developments at m2. First and foremost, a brand new white wine for m2, hitherto known only for ballsy reds: a 2012 Torrontés, picked this past mid-August from Ron Silva’s acclaimed Silvaspoons Vineyards in Lodi’s Alta Mesa AVA. One taste of the settling, unfiltered, golden colored juice – bursting with tropical flower, grapefruit and pineapple fruit qualities, tasting bone dry and tart edged, while fleshy and flush in exotic fruit qualities in the mouth – told us that this could very well become a signature white wine for m2, and maybe Lodi in general.
“We’d been looking for a white wine unique enough to mean something special,” says Montgomery, who also did his homework before tackling this exotic grape – including, picking the brain of veteran winemaker Ken Volks (of Kenneth Volks Vineyards in Santa Barbara, and former owner of Wild Horse Winery), whose Torrontés took “Best White Wine in California” honors at the 2012 California State Fair.
During the weekend before (October 20-21), Montgomery had just received the last of his 2012 Zinfandel crop from Maley Vineyards and Mohr-Fry Ranches – nearly six weeks after receiving his first bins of Zinfandel from Soucie Vineyard as well as a “new” old vine planting he is splitting with Fields Family Wines for the first time this year – a 107 year old vineyard located on Kettleman at Alpine they are calling the Century Block.
Because we were thirsty, we ended our visit with a taste of the currently released 2010 m2 Artist Series Lodi Zinfandel ($35): a more sculpted, studied style (blended with Maley, Soucie and Mohr-Fry fruit) than that of the usually wild and wooly m2 Soucie zins – in this case, sporting a lusciously sweet toned blackberry aroma nuanced with raspberry preserves, tasting thick, dense, juicy and consistently layered on the palate. Another m2 winner!

Montgomery's new white wine, a 2012 Torrontés, has bursts of tropical fruit flavour and tartness, making it a potential signature white wine for m2 Wines and Lodi. Finally, m2 Wines has released a 2010 Artist Series Lodi Zinfandel, blended with fruit from Maley, Soucie, and Mohr-Fry vineyards, which has a luscious, sweet blackberry aroma and is consistently layered on the palate.
